title: The Vanished Star
subtitle: A Color By Number Mystery
setting: Larkspur Hollow, a river town of crooked roofs and one tall fir. Every winter, on the evening of the Starlight Fair, the Founders' Star is lit on top of that fir. Twelve neighbours had a key, a reason or a chance to be in the square last night.
intro: You are the town's volunteer detective, and you have until dusk. Each chapter hides one piece of evidence inside a colour-by-number mosaic. Colour it to see WHAT was found. Solve the two puzzles to learn WHAT IT WAS LIKE. Then the evidence card tells you what that proves, and one more neighbour is in the clear.

suspects.name: Wren the lamplighter
suspects.about: lights every street lamp at dusk; her grandfather forged the star

suspects.name: Mabel the baker
suspects.about: bakes the Fair's star buns; lost the stall lottery this year

suspects.name: Otis the clockmaker
suspects.about: keeps the tower clock; says the star throws his chimes off

suspects.name: Pippa the florist
suspects.about: dresses the fir each winter; argued with the Mayor on Friday

suspects.name: Hugo the ferryman
suspects.about: runs the river ferry; a quiet Fair means no fares

suspects.name: Nell the librarian
suspects.about: keeps the town records; knows what the charter says about the star

suspects.name: Basil the choirmaster
suspects.about: leads the chapel choir; wanted the star moved to the chapel roof

suspects.name: Ivy the toymaker
suspects.about: builds wind-up toys; once asked to copy the star's points

suspects.name: Tobias the postman
suspects.about: delivers the post before dawn; first across the square each day

suspects.name: Greta the weaver
suspects.about: weaves the Fair banners; her loom shed faces the fir

suspects.name: Felix the fiddler
suspects.about: plays for the dances; owes the Fair committee for a broken stage

suspects.name: Dora the cobbler
suspects.about: mends the town's shoes; her shop window looks onto the square

chapters.title: A Thread on the Fir
chapters.story:
7:25 a.m. The square is blue with early light. The fir stands where it always has, but its top is bare, and the hook that held the star swings in the wind.
Pip tugs your sleeve. "There. See it?" High on the last branch, something flutters: a single thread, caught on the bark, bright against the snow.
Greta the weaver is already underneath, squinting up. "That is not from my banners," she says quickly. Too quickly? Mabel the baker folds her arms. "Well, it is not from my apron either."
Everyone in Larkspur Hollow wraps up against the cold. Whoever climbed up there left a piece of themselves behind. You fetch the long apple-picker from the bakery yard and bring the thread down, turning it in your fingers.
What did it come from? What is it made of? And what colour is it, once the frost is brushed away? Three questions, three puzzles.
chapters.scene: Snowy town square at dawn, a tall fir tree with an empty top, a thread caught on a branch
chapters.meaning: The thread was pulled from a red wool scarf. Whoever took the star wore a red scarf.

decoys.meaning: The thread is from the chapel bell rope. Whoever took the star had been ringing with the choir.
A silk scarf, far too fine for this town. The taker came over from the south bank.
A yellow wool thread from the festival bunting. It tells you nothing about the taker.

side.intro: Decode the witness statement. One word in it describes the evidence: the evidence card shows which.
side.message: The weaver felt the thread and said it was spun from thick woollen yarn

side.intro: Follow the trail through the maze. The letters on your path spell a word that describes the evidence.

chapters.evidence: What did the thread come from, and what was it like?
hints: Colour every cell marked 1 first: the darkest colour draws the picture.
The picture is something you wear in winter. Decode the statement to learn what it is made of.
The mosaic shows a SCARF. The keywords are WOOLLEN and CRIMSON.
chapters.teaser: One thread, and your list is already shorter. But a thread cannot tell you how anyone found the star's brass label in the pitch dark. Pip can. He is still hopping. "Ask me what I SAW," he says.

chapters.title: Sharp Eyes
chapters.story:
7:50 a.m. Pip drags you to the bakery and points up at his attic window.
"I could not sleep, because of the buns. So I looked out. The lamps were out and the square was black. Then somebody was standing under the fir, holding up a little light. They held the star out at arm's length, like this, and read the label on its back. Then the light went away."
"Read it? From that far?" The label on the Founders' Star is a strip of brass the size of your thumb, engraved by the smith who made it.
Otis the clockmaker, passing with his toolbox, snorts. "Nobody reads engraving by night. I cannot read it at noon without my lenses." Greta nods hard and pushes her own spectacles up her nose.
So what was the light the figure carried, how strong was it, and how big are those letters really? If Pip is telling the truth, the answer says something about the taker's eyes.
chapters.scene: A brass label on a golden star, a child peeking from a bakery window at night
chapters.meaning: Tiny letters, read from arm's length by a faint light: sharp eyes. The taker does not wear glasses.

decoys.meaning: The figure was only checking the time on the tower. It was a choir singer late for practice.
A blazing light like that belongs to the ferry. The taker lives on the south side.
Anyone can read huge letters, even by a faint light. Nothing is proved.

side.intro: Decode the witness statement. One word in it describes the evidence: the evidence card shows which.
side.message: The boy said the small light in that hand was faint and yellow

side.intro: Follow the trail through the maze. The letters on your path spell a word that describes the evidence.

chapters.evidence: What did the figure hold, and what do your keywords say about that night?
hints: The picture is something you carry in the dark.
Decode the statement: its last word is the first keyword. The second keyword lies along your path.
The mosaic shows a LANTERN. The keywords are FAINT and TINY.
chapters.teaser: Good eyes, then. That clears the spectacle wearers, and it makes Pip's story true. So does the snow: it stopped falling at eleven last night, and nobody has swept the square since.

chapters.title: Prints in the Snow
chapters.story:
8:30 a.m. You should have looked down sooner. From the corner by the pump, one clean trail crosses the white square to the foot of the fir, and one trail leads away again.
"Do not step on it!" Dora the cobbler comes running out of her shop in her felt clogs, a measuring ribbon round her neck. She kneels by the clearest mark like a doctor by a patient.
"Deep," she mutters. "Somebody heavy, or somebody carrying something." The star weighs as much as a full milk churn.
Pippa the florist watches from her doorway in soft indoor shoes, hugging herself. "I never left my shop," she says, though nobody asked.
Dora stretches the ribbon along the mark, reads the number, then runs a finger over the pattern pressed into the snow. She smiles a small, sure smile. "I know exactly what made this. And I can tell you its size."
chapters.scene: A trail of prints crossing fresh snow toward a fir tree, a cobbler kneeling with a ribbon
chapters.meaning: Size 44 prints with ridged soles: a grown-up's heavy winter boots. The taker wore boots.

decoys.meaning: The trail was made by a large animal, not a person. Only someone with a cat would be followed like that.
Size 28 is a child's boot. No grown-up in the dossier fits.
Smooth soles slip on a ladder. The taker climbed without one.

side.intro: Open the cobbler's measuring lock. The code is the size of what made the trail.
Follow the trail through the maze. The letters on your path spell a word that describes the evidence.

chapters.evidence: What made the trail, what size was it, and what was its sole like?
hints: The picture is something you wear outdoors.
It goes on a foot. Work each dial from left to right for its size.
The mosaic shows a BOOT. The keywords are 44 and RIDGED.
chapters.teaser: Dora's ribbon clears the soft-shoed, Dora included. But a trail starts somewhere. You follow it backwards, past the pump, down Ferry Lane, towards the river. If it crosses the water, half the town is suspect again.

chapters.title: The River Crossing
chapters.story:
9:40 a.m. The river cuts Larkspur Hollow in two. North bank: the square, the chapel, the fir. South bank: the ferry house, the dance hall, the mill. One old stone crossing joins them, with an iron gate in the middle that the ferryman locks in bad weather.
Hugo the ferryman meets you there, breath smoking. "You think one of us southerners carried it over? Look for yourself."
Felix the fiddler leans on the rail behind him, fiddle case on his back. "I was playing at the hall till two. Ask anyone."
Hugo opens his logbook to last night. He walked down at dusk and again at dawn, and wrote what he found both times. The trail of prints, you notice, stops well before the river and turns back towards the square.
On the gatepost somebody has pinned a scrap of card. Four words, in careful capitals: IT WILL COME BACK.
What did Hugo inspect, and in what state did he find it? If nobody could cross, the taker sleeps on this side of the water.
chapters.scene: A small stone crossing over a river at night, warm windows on the north bank
chapters.meaning: The bridge gate was frozen in its frame and shut from dusk to dawn. Nobody crossed: the taker lives on the north side.

decoys.meaning: A ladder lay across the river ice like a walkway. Only someone in soft shoes could cross it without slipping: the taker wore no boots.
The gate was shut, but a left-handed latch opens it from outside. The taker is left-handed.
The crossing stood open. Anyone from either bank could have come.

side.intro: Decode the witness statement. One word in it describes the evidence: the evidence card shows which.
side.message: The ferryman wrote in his log that the river gate was frozen from dusk to dawn

side.intro: Follow the trail through the maze. The letters on your path spell a word that describes the evidence.

chapters.evidence: What did the ferryman look at, and how did he find it?
hints: The picture is something that stands over water.
Decode the statement for the first keyword. The maze path spells the second.
The mosaic shows a BRIDGE. The keywords are FROZEN and SHUT.
chapters.teaser: Nobody crossed. The taker lives north of the river, and somebody wants you to stop looking. IT WILL COME BACK. Who writes that about a stolen star? You walk back to the fir with the card in your pocket.

chapters.title: Two Marks in the Bark
chapters.story:
10:55 a.m. Six hours to dusk. The Mayor is pacing the square, and the stallholders have stopped unpacking.
You circle the fir slowly. The star hung four times as high as a tall man, and the lowest branches would not hold a cat. Nobody simply reached up.
Near the foot of the trunk, on the side away from the bakery, the bark is scraped pale in two places, a hand's width each, side by side. Two matching dents sit in the snow below them.
Nell the librarian has come out with the charter under her arm. "I looked it up," she says. "The star may only be taken down by the town, with the town's own steps, in daylight." She frowns at the dents. "These are not the town's. Those are kept in the chapel, and they are much too big."
The carpenter crouches beside you and picks something out of the bark with his thumbnail.
What leaned here, what is it made of, and how far apart are its feet?
chapters.scene: Close view of a fir trunk with two dents in the snow-dusted bark
chapters.meaning: A narrow wooden ladder stood against the tree, the kind kept in a shed. The taker owns a ladder.

decoys.meaning: The dents are only old knots in the trunk. The taker climbed the branches in soft shoes, not boots.
An iron ladder is the ferry's own. The taker lives on the south side.
A broad wooden ladder is the one from the chapel. The taker sings in the choir.

side.intro: Decode the witness statement. One word in it describes the evidence: the evidence card shows which.
side.message: The carpenter found splinters in the bark so both rails were wooden for sure

side.intro: Follow the trail through the maze. The letters on your path spell a word that describes the evidence.

chapters.evidence: What leaned against the tree, and what was it like?
hints: The picture is a tool for reaching high places.
Decode the statement: it names what the tool is made of.
The mosaic shows a LADDER. The keywords are WOODEN and NARROW.
chapters.teaser: Whoever owns one of those climbed the fir at midnight, alone. And midnight is exactly when the chapel windows were bright and full of singing.

chapters.title: The Midnight Rehearsal
chapters.story:
12:10 p.m. The chapel smells of candle wax and oranges. Basil the choirmaster is stacking hymn books with sharp little slaps.
"I asked for that star on our roof, yes. Asked. In writing. I do not creep about in the dark." He nods at the music stand. "We practised from ten until one. Every singer signed the sheet when we began the last piece, as we always do. Read it."
A sheet of paper lies on the stand, covered in signatures. Felix's is there, with a flourish. So is Basil's. In the corner the choirmaster has written the time they signed.
Pip counts on his fingers. "The tower struck twelve just as the little light went out. I heard it."
So everything hangs on that corner of the page. What exactly were they singing, and at what time did every one of them put a name to it? If the two times match, the choir was all in one room, and the taker was not.
chapters.scene: A candle-lit chapel with singers, a sheet on a stand, a clock showing midnight
chapters.meaning: The carol sheet was signed by every singer at 12:00, the very minute the star vanished. The taker is not in the choir.

decoys.meaning: The bell that rang a carol at 12:00 hangs on the south bank. The taker lives on the south side.
A lullaby is sung at home with a cat on the lap. The taker keeps a cat.
The sheet was signed at 10:30, long before the star vanished. It proves nothing.

side.intro: Decode the witness statement. One word in it describes the evidence: the evidence card shows which.
side.message: The page on the stand was the old winter carol the town sings each year

side.intro: Open the chapel clock case. The code is the time written on the sheet.

chapters.evidence: What lay on the stand, what was sung, and at what time was it signed?
hints: The picture is something you can sing.
Decode the statement for the first keyword. The dials give a time of four digits.
The mosaic shows a music NOTE. The keywords are CAROL and 1200.
chapters.teaser: The singers are clear, every one. You are close enough now that somebody is nervous: as you leave the chapel, a shutter across the square clicks closed.

chapters.title: Dropped in the Snow
chapters.story:
1:35 p.m. Three and a half hours. A cloud bank is climbing over the mill, the colour of slate.
Under the lowest branch of the fir, half buried, Pip finds it: something dropped in a hurry, stiff with frost. He holds it up like a trophy.
Old Captain Marsh, who teaches knots at the school, takes it from him and turns it over twice. Then he looks up at the rope that held the star. "Untied, not cut," he says. "Neat work. Whoever did it took this off to feel the knot, and never picked it up again."
Ivy the toymaker has drifted over from her workshop, wiping oil from her fingers. "May I see?" She reaches for it with her left hand, then stops, and puts both hands in her pockets.
The Captain tries the thing on, first one hand, then the other. "Hm," he says. "That settles which hand does the work."
What was dropped, how heavy is its cloth, and which hand does it fit?
chapters.scene: An old sailor examining a small found object beside a rope tied to a fir branch
chapters.meaning: A thick glove for the right hand, worn thin from work. The taker is not left-handed.

decoys.meaning: A thick key that turns to the right: the chapel key. The taker is in the choir.
A thin indoor glove. The taker had no winter boots on either.
A thick left-hand glove with a spectacle cloth tucked inside. The taker wears glasses.

side.intro: Follow the trail through the maze. The letters on your path spell a word that describes the evidence.
Decode the witness statement. One word in it describes the evidence: the evidence card shows which.
side.message: The sailor tried it on both hands and it only fits the right one

chapters.evidence: What was dropped, and which one was it?
hints: The picture is something you wear, but not on your feet.
It has five fingers. Decode the statement to learn which hand.
The mosaic shows a GLOVE. The keywords are THICK and RIGHT.
chapters.teaser: Your list is very short now, and you do not like either name on it. Then Pip, who never looks where grown-ups look, says: "Why are there TWO trails?"

chapters.title: The Last Trace
chapters.story:
2:50 p.m. He is right. Beside the deep prints runs a second, smaller trail that you took for windblown snow. It trots along next to the first, wanders off to sniff the pump, comes back, and sits, you can see the round hollow, at the foot of the fir, waiting.
The taker was not alone. Something kept them company.
Doctor Hale, the vet, kneels with her lamp although it is daylight. "Small. Four toes." She tilts the lamp. "And look at the tips."
Tobias the postman has stopped his round to watch. His big grey cat, Button, rides in the post bag as always, glaring at everyone. "Button never leaves this bag," Tobias says. "Ask the whole town."
The first flakes of new snow are coming down. In an hour this trail will be gone for good.
What left it, what shape are the marks, and what do the tips of the toes show? One last fact, and only one neighbour fits them all.
chapters.scene: A vet with a lamp examining small marks in the snow, a friendly animal waiting by a door
chapters.meaning: Wide paw prints with claw marks: a dog walked beside the taker. A cat hides its claws, so the taker does not keep a cat.

decoys.meaning: The marks are where the star itself was dragged. The taker pulled it with the left hand.
Soft prints with no claw marks are slippers, not paws. The taker wore no boots.
Narrow clawed prints belong to a fox passing by. They say nothing about the taker.

side.intro: Decode the witness statement. One word in it describes the evidence: the evidence card shows which.
side.message: The vet saw four toes and sharp points at each tip so the feet were clawed

side.intro: Follow the trail through the maze. The letters on your path spell a word that describes the evidence.

chapters.evidence: What left the second trail, and what were the marks like?
hints: The picture is a print left by an animal.
Decode the statement for the first keyword. The maze path tells how broad the marks were.
The mosaic shows a PAW. The keywords are CLAWED and WIDE.
chapters.teaser: Eight facts. Open your Code Log. Somewhere in Larkspur Hollow, behind a closed shutter, a hammer is tapping very softly, and the tower clock says ten past three.

finale:
3:10 p.m. Twelve neighbours, eight facts. Go through your Code Log and cross out everyone who does not fit a fact. One name stays.
Before you knock on that door, think about the card on the gatepost. IT WILL COME BACK. This was never a theft for money. So why would this neighbour, of all people, carry the Founders' Star home in the middle of the night?
epilogue:
4:40 p.m. The door opens before you knock. On the workbench inside, under a lamp, lies the Founders' Star, and one of its five points is bright with new solder.
"It cracked in the autumn storm," your neighbour says. "One more night of wind and that point would have come down on the square. If the council had known, there would have been no star this year, and no Fair, and you know what happens to the fir then. So I took it down myself, in the dark, and I have not slept since." A tail thumps under the bench.
At five o'clock exactly, with the whole town holding its breath, the star goes up the fir again. It has never shone so brightly.
Who was it? You know the name. Prove it in the Case Vault to unlock the portrait and the last page of the story.
prologue:
The knocking starts at ten past seven. On your doorstep stands Mayor Alder, hat in his hands, snow on his shoulders.
"It's gone," he says. "The Founders' Star. A hundred winters on top of that fir, and this morning there is nothing but sky."
You know what that means. The town charter says it plainly: no star, no Starlight Fair. And without the Fair the timber company's offer for the old fir, the one the council has refused nine years running, goes to a vote on Monday.
"Somebody took it in the night," the Mayor whispers. "Somebody who knew the square. One of us." He presses a folded list into your hand. Twelve names. You have bought bread from them, borrowed books from them, sung beside them.
Behind him, half hidden by the gate, a small boy in a flour-dusted apron is hopping from foot to foot. Pip, the baker's boy. "I saw something," he blurts. "Last night. From my window."
The tower clock strikes the quarter. Dusk falls at five. If the star is not shining by then, the Fair is over before it begins, and the fir may never see another winter.
You pull on your coat. "Show me," you say.
